title: Base Camp One: the pitch and the stranger test
summary: They pitch the product to the family with the prototype and the plan and take their questions, then a person who was never in the room runs their programs from the README alone while their hands stay in their pockets.
materials: your prototype, at whatever stage it honestly is
the shop idea page and the plan sheet you have been filling in
the laptop, with your programs and your README open
the repo link, sent by the parent who holds the account
a stranger: someone who was never in the room, on a video call or in person, at their own computer
paper and pencil for the family's questions and for the stalls
the Maker's Log and the bug diary

steps.title: Base Camp One
steps.body:
Three weeks ago Python lived on a micro:bit and the shop was one line on an idea page. Today the sprint gets weighed, and it gets weighed by other people, which is the only weighing that counts.

Two events, in this order. First the pitch: five minutes, your prototype on the table, your plan beside it, and then the family asks questions. Second the stranger test: someone who was never in this room opens your README and runs your programs from it alone, and your hands stay in your pockets the whole time.

The design loop still runs the day, aimed at a new question. Ask: does this plan survive contact with people who are not me? Imagine every place a stranger could stumble: a step you never wrote down, a file name only you know, a word that means something to you and nothing to them. Plan: you cannot rehearse the stranger, so you rehearse the README instead. Read it once, out loud, pretending you have never seen your own laptop.

One house rule for the pitch, and it is the family's rule as much as yours: they question the plan, never the choice. What you decided to make is yours. How you plan to make it, price it and finish it is fair game, and the harder they push there, the better the plan gets.

One last thing before you turn the page. Hand the device to a grown-up when you reach the next step. It is addressed to them and to the stranger, not to you, and a stranger test you have already read the script for is not a test.

steps.title: For the family and the stranger only
steps.body:
Family, this step is addressed to you. Hand the device back after reading it.

At the pitch, cross-examine the plan and leave the choice alone. Good questions sound like these: how long does one unit take you to make, and how do you know? What does one cost you in materials? What happens if the first three come out badly? Who exactly is going to buy this, and have you asked any of them? What is your price a guess about? Bad questions sound like why did you not make something better, or nobody would buy that. The product is theirs, and a season built on their choice does not get to relitigate it at week 4. Push on the plan until it creaks; that is the gift.

Stranger, your job is harder than it sounds: follow the README exactly, and do not be helpful. Do not guess what they meant. Do not fill in a missing step from common sense. When you reach something the page does not tell you, stop and say out loud what you were looking for and could not find, then wait. Silence while you are stuck is the most valuable thing that happens today, so please be willing to look stuck in front of a child this age. They are not allowed to talk you through it; they are allowed to rewrite the page and hand it back.

One setup note: the repo lives on a parent-held account, so a parent sends you the link. If Python is not on your computer, try what the README says about that first. If getting it installed is going to eat the whole visit, a parent may sit with you for the install and only the install, and they write down that their page could not carry that step alone yet.

Five minutes on your typing site before anyone sits down. Warm up on the home row, then type the sprint's own words, ten times each, without looking down: print, input, int, open, git, add, commit, push, readme. Every one of them is on the laptop that is about to be used by somebody else, and steady fingers make a calmer demo.

steps.title: Why the builder is the worst tester
steps.body:
There is a reason today needs a stranger and not just another careful read by you.

Psychologists ran an experiment where one person tapped the rhythm of a famous song on a table and another person listened and tried to name it. Before each tap, the tappers guessed how many listeners would get it: about half, they said. Almost nobody did, closer to one listener in forty. Inside the tapper's head the whole song was playing, words, tune, drums and all. Outside, on the table, there was nothing but knocking.

That gap has a name in engineering: once you know something, you cannot feel what not knowing it is like. Your README is a tapped song. You know that the program has to be run from the folder its data file sits in, that the numbers in that file go one per line, that typing 1200 m instead of 1200 stops int dead. None of that is on the page, because your head keeps supplying it for free every time you read it.

There is no trick that fixes this from the inside. Reading it again does not work; you will hear the tune again. The only instrument that measures the gap is a person who does not have the song in their head, sitting at a keyboard, doing exactly what the page says. That is what walks in today, and every place they stall is a real measurement, not an accident and not their fault.

figure.alt: The pitch layout: the prototype sits on the table with the one-page plan beside it, you stand to present, and the family sits facing you to ask questions once the five minutes are up.

steps.title: The pitch
steps.body:
Five minutes, no slides, prototype on the table. Whatever you are making, the pitch answers the same four questions.

One: what is it, and who is it for? Say it in one sentence a stranger could repeat. Two: what does one of them cost you to make, and what do you think you can charge? Both numbers are first guesses today; weeks 5 and 6 turn them into real ones, and saying out loud that a number is a guess is a strength, not a wobble. Three: how many can you actually finish with the time and the materials you have? Count the hours you really have, not the hours you wish for. Four: what could go wrong, and what would you do about it?

Then hand the floor over and take the questions. Write down every question you cannot answer yet; that list is the real output of the pitch, and it becomes next week's work. If a question stings a little, write it down twice.
checklist: I said what it is, who it is for, and what one costs me to make
I gave a price and said out loud which parts of it are still a guess
I said how many I can really finish, from hours I actually have
Every question I could not answer is written down, in their words

steps.title: The stranger test
steps.body:
Now the drama. Someone who was never in this room opens your README and runs your programs from it, and you say nothing.

Set it up cleanly: a parent sends them the link, they open the page on their own computer, and you put your hands in your pockets and leave them there. Not folded, not near the keyboard. Pockets. Watch their screen if you can see it, and watch their face if you cannot.

When they stall, do not rescue them. Write down what they were looking for, in their words, not the words you wish they had used. A stall is a measurement, and this one only happens once, because in ten minutes you will know too much again.

Then the part that is the whole point: fix the page on the spot. Open the README, write the missing step, save it, commit it with a message that says why, and push it, because until you push, the page they are looking at is still the old one. Then ask them to reload and start again from the top. Rewriting your instructions in front of someone while they wait is not embarrassing. It is what shipping actually looks like, and a stranger who stalls twice on the same line has given you a better afternoon than a stranger who sails through.

If the run finishes, ask them one last question: was there any moment where you thought about giving up? Write down the answer.
checklist: The person had never seen the program before, and nothing went to them but the link a parent sent
My hands stayed in my pockets while they worked
Every stall went into the bug diary in their words, not mine
I fixed the README on the spot, committed and pushed it, and they reloaded the page and started again from the top
I wrote down how far the second run got, however far that was

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Record the moment that matters: the stall, the fix, and the rerun. If a camera is awkward, a photo of the README before and after, or the two versions pasted as text, tells the same story. Add one line saying which stall you would never have found alone.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
